newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco liability may top asbestos - trade group.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco liability may top asbestos - trade group.

text.p: Tobacco-related claims could cost the U.S. insurance industry more than $250 billion, a potentially worse blow than the one delivered by asbestos in the late 1980s, an insurance trade group said on Wednesday.

"It's going to be huge," Richard Hodyl, insurance services counsel with the National Association of Independent Insurers said in a telephone interview. "This is going to be a big deal. It's here and it's now," he added.
But others in the insurance industry said it was far too early to estimate the potential liability for insurers.
"At this point, we'd be quite sceptical of figures at all," said Sean Mooney, senior vice president for the Insurance Information Institute.
"And if such a figure were to be put forward, we would expect, at this stage, it would be relatively lower," he said.
The insurance industry has argued that policies sold to tobacco companies after the mid-1960s exclude payment for losses related to the harmful effects of smoking.
In addition, Mooney said, there would be strong arguments to deny coverage of policies sold before the mid-1960s.
But Hodyl said he told an NAII claims committee meeting on June 12 that tobacco-related claims may come from outside the tobacco industry as well as tobacco companies themselves.

The NAII represents more than 560 property-casualty insurance companies nationwide. The Insurance Information Institute is a communications organisation sponsored by the U.S. property-casualty insurance industry.
Wholesalers, retail stores that sell tobacco products and media that design and display public advertising may seek coverage under their liability policies, Hodyl said.
Thus, he said, a liability insurer may have substantial exposure arising from tobacco litigation even though it never insured a tobacco company.

And although tobacco companies have so far shied away from submitting liability claims to their insurers, that may change as the number of lawsuits rises and tobacco investors force the companies to seek reimbursement from their insurers, he said.
Tobacco companies have been reluctant to pursue their insurers for coverage because they have wanted to maintain complete control over their legal defences, he said.

State attorneys general have been negotiating a settlement to litigation that some reports say could reach $250 billion to $300 billion over 25 years. A settlement could be announced as early as Thursday, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a key negotiator, said late Wednesday.
But the American Insurance Association, a trade group representing more than 300 predominantly commercial property-casualty insurers, said it does not believe it has any tobacco liability.
"It is our belief that insurers have no liability in this matter -- none," AIA spokesman Dan Zielinski said.
